title: Venous Access Device Manufacturing
one_liner: U.S. venous access device manufacturers make PICCs, central venous catheters, implantable ports, dialysis catheters, securement products, connectors and related access technology used to deliver drugs, fluids, nutrition, chemotherapy and dialysis.
overview: This industry manufactures devices used to access a patient's venous bloodstream, including peripherally inserted central catheters, central venous catheters, dialysis catheters, implantable ports, Huber needles, securement devices, needleless connectors, disinfection caps and placement-support technologies. The 2021 baseline file placed U.S. industry revenue at $6.496 billion in 2021 and projected $6.9 billion in 2026, implying a 2021-2026 CAGR of about 1.2%. Current 2025-2026 evidence points to steady rather than breakout growth: CMS projects national health expenditure growth of 5.4% annually over 2025-2034, Grand View Research estimates the broader U.S. vascular access devices market at $4.3787 billion in 2024 with 4.4% CAGR from 2025-2030, and suppliers such as BD and Teleflex continue reporting growth in vascular access and vascular product lines. The market remains concentrated around diversified medtech companies whose vascular access lines sit inside broader medication delivery, interventional, infusion therapy and hospital consumables portfolios.

baseline_2022.market_size: 2022: about $6.57 billion estimated U.S. venous access device manufacturing revenue, calculated from the baseline file's 2021 revenue of $6.496 billion and 2021-2026 CAGR of 1.2%.
baseline_2022.growth: 2022: about 1.2% estimated year-over-year growth, consistent with the baseline file's 2021-2026 forecast path.

how_it_makes_money: Manufacturers sell sterile single-use and semi-durable venous access products to hospitals, outpatient centers, oncology clinics, dialysis providers, distributors and group purchasing organization contracts. Revenue comes from device unit sales, procedural kits, recurring consumables such as connectors, caps and securement products, premium antimicrobial or power-injectable catheters, port-access needles, placement technology, training and contract supply agreements. Large firms also cross-sell venous access products with infusion pumps, IV solutions, medication delivery platforms and broader hospital consumables.
cost_structure: Major costs are resin, polyurethane, silicone, stainless-steel needles, coatings, packaging, sterilization, cleanroom manufacturing labor, quality systems, FDA compliance, product-liability insurance, R&D, salesforce support and distributor or GPO rebates. The 2021 baseline showed a 10.3% profit margin, while BD's 2025 filing points to continuing pressure from tariffs, labor and raw materials partly offset by manufacturing productivity and supply-chain optimization. Buyers remain price-sensitive because GPOs and health systems aggregate purchasing volume, but premium products can earn higher margins when they reduce infection risk, restarts, line failures or imaging costs.
major_players: Becton, Dickinson and Company / Bard Access Systems
current_dynamics: Demand in 2025-2026 is being pulled by procedure volumes, oncology infusion, dialysis, hospital medication delivery, difficult vascular access programs and infection-prevention protocols. BD reported 2025 volume growth in its Medication Delivery Solutions vascular access management portfolio, and Teleflex reported $917.7 million of 2025 vascular revenue with 2026 continuing-operations revenue growth guidance of 4.5%-5.5% on a pro forma constant-currency basis. At the same time, device recalls and FDA scrutiny are keeping quality systems front-and-center, while hospital consolidation and GPO contracting limit manufacturers' ability to pass through every increase in labor, resin, sterilization and tariff-related costs.
whats_growing: Antimicrobial and infection-prevention catheters, passive-safety peripheral IV catheters, midline catheters, power-injectable PICCs, ultrasound-guided deeper-access products, catheter securement, needleless connectors, disinfection caps and port-access consumables are growing. The 2025 U.S. antimicrobial catheters market estimate of $506.18 million and 2026-2033 CAGR of 7.94% show the premium infection-control segment outpacing the mature core catheter market.
whats_shrinking: Commodity conventional catheters, undifferentiated access kits and products exposed to direct GPO price comparisons are losing relative share. Legacy products face substitution from longer-dwell peripheral IVs, midlines, antimicrobial devices and better visualization or tip-location tools. Domestic manufacturers also face pressure where imports or offshore production can meet hospital specifications at lower cost.
recent_developments: 2025-03-11: BD subsidiary Bard initiated a recall of certain 4 Fr Single-Lumen PowerPICC catheters because tubing outside melt-flow specifications could increase fatigue leaks and therapy interruption risk.
2025-07-01: FDA cleared Access Vascular's Dual Lumen 5Fr HydroPICC Catheter under 510(k) K251212.
2025-11-25: BD's 2025 Form 10-K reported 2025 volume growth in Medication Delivery Solutions' vascular access management portfolio.
2026-01-05: FDA classified the Bard PowerPICC action as a Class I recall after an April 18, 2025 early alert.
2026-02-27: Teleflex reported $917.7 million of 2025 vascular revenue and guided 2026 continuing-operations revenue growth of 4.5%-5.5% on a pro forma constant-currency basis.
2026-06-24: CMS released updated projections showing 2025-2034 national health expenditure growth averaging 5.4% annually.
outlook: Through 2030, the industry should grow modestly in manufacturing revenue and faster in premium niches. The 2026 U.S. manufacturing revenue base is about $6.9 billion under the baseline forecast, while the broader U.S. vascular access devices market is projected to rise from $4.3787 billion in 2024 to $5.6996 billion in 2030. Growth will come less from basic catheter volume and more from mix shift: antimicrobial coatings, longer-dwell devices, power injection, midlines, ultrasound-guided placement, tip confirmation and securement. Downside risks are product recalls, purchasing concentration, reimbursement pressure, tariff and raw-material inflation, and substitution away from central lines when lower-risk peripheral options are clinically acceptable.
themes: Aging population and chronic disease sustain procedure demand
Oncology and dialysis support long-term access volumes
Infection prevention raises willingness to pay for antimicrobial and closed-access products
Hospitals use GPOs to pressure pricing and standardize product formularies
Quality systems and recalls are material competitive risks
Manufacturers compete through bundles that combine catheters, securement, connectors, disinfection and placement support
Midlines and longer-dwell peripheral IVs can reduce use of more invasive central access in selected patients
one_sentence: The industry is mature but resilient: 2026 demand is supported by higher U.S. health spending, cancer care, kidney disease and infection-prevention upgrades, while hospital purchasing groups, recalls, tariffs and lower-cost imports keep pricing pressure high.

title: Venture Capital & Principal Trading in the US
one_liner: A volatile finance industry where venture investors and proprietary traders earn returns from startup stakes, securities positions, spreads, exits and financial contracts.
overview: This industry covers firms and individuals acting as principals in financial markets, including venture capital companies, investment clubs, securities speculators, tax-lien dealers, mineral and oil royalty dealers, mortgage dealers and viatical settlement companies. The 2022 IBISWorld baseline put industry revenue at $63.0 billion, with venture capitalists and financial-product traders together representing more than 90% of revenue. By 2025-2026, the industry was being pulled in two directions: venture deal value rebounded sharply because AI companies absorbed very large rounds, while broader VC fundraising and exits remained below the 2021 peak; at the same time, principal traders benefited from elevated equity, options and derivatives volumes during tariff, rates and geopolitical volatility.

key_stats.market_size: 2026 projected industry revenue: about $70.5 billion, calculated from the 2022 IBISWorld baseline of $63.0 billion at its 2022-2028 projected 2.83% CAGR.
key_stats.growth: 2022-2028 projected industry revenue CAGR: 2.83%; 2025 US VC capital deployed rose 51% to $320 billion; 2025 US equities ADV rose 44.6% year over year to 17.6 billion shares.
key_stats.profit_margin: 2022 baseline profit margin: 42.9%, equal to $27.0 billion of profit on $63.0 billion of revenue.
key_stats.employment: 2022 baseline employment: 94,959 workers; 2027 baseline forecast: 111,098 workers.
key_stats.vc_activity: 2025 US VC deployed $320 billion across 15,352 deals, with AI accounting for 65.4% of deal value.
key_stats.trading_activity: Q2 2026 US equity ADV was 20.2 billion shares and options ADV was 72.8 million contracts, both described by SIFMA as record highs.

baseline_2022.growth: 2022 revenue growth: 7.6%; 2017-2022 revenue CAGR: 11.3%; 2022-2028 projected CAGR: 2.83%.
baseline_2022.segments: 2022 revenue split: venture capitalists 48.2%, traders in financial products 45.1%, other investors 6.7%.

how_it_makes_money: Operators earn money from capital gains on securities and financial contracts, bid-ask spreads, proprietary trading profits, venture fund management and carried interest, gains on VC-backed IPOs and M&A exits, sales of royalty interests, tax-lien dealing and discounted settlement investments. Venture capital economics depend on fund fees, investment appreciation and exits; principal trading economics depend on volatility, liquidity, market access, pricing models, leverage and turnover.
cost_structure: The 2022 baseline showed a high-margin model: profit was 42.9% of revenue and wages were $14.529 billion, or about 23.1% of revenue. Major costs include compensation for investment professionals, traders, engineers and compliance staff; technology, data, exchange connectivity and clearing; interest and financing costs for leveraged positions; legal, fund administration, audit and regulatory costs; occupancy and insurance. Cost pressure in 2025-2026 is coming from AI and quant talent compensation, data infrastructure, cybersecurity, regulatory reporting and higher-for-longer financing costs.
current_dynamics: The industry is no longer broadly buoyed by the zero-rate VC cycle. In 2025, capital flowed heavily to a small number of AI and infrastructure companies, while many software, consumer and life-science startups still faced slower follow-on rounds and muted exits. In trading, elevated equity and options volumes, off-exchange trading and derivatives activity increased opportunities for market makers and proprietary traders. The common thread is concentration: large VC platforms with dry powder, top AI issuers and leading electronic trading firms are capturing a greater share of activity.
whats_growing: AI venture rounds, mega-deals, early-stage AI infrastructure, secondaries, continuation vehicles, private-credit-backed liquidity, US IPO issuance, off-exchange equity trading, short-dated options, derivatives volumes and electronic market-making capacity are growing in 2025-2026.
whats_shrinking: Traditional VC fundraising breadth, the number of closed VC funds, non-AI venture allocation, weaker late-stage companies, speculative 2021-era valuations and small-manager access to LP commitments are shrinking or lagging. Principal traders with weaker technology, less scale or higher leverage face margin pressure as competition and compliance costs rise.
recent_developments: 2025: US venture capital deployed $320 billion across 15,352 deals, up 51% year over year, with AI taking 65.4% of deal value.
2025: US VC fundraising totaled $67 billion, the lowest level in 9 years, despite strong headline deployment.
2025: US IPO activity rose 55% year over year to 349 IPOs including SPACs, raising $75.5 billion in proceeds.
2025: US equities average daily volume increased 44.6% year over year to 17.6 billion shares, with average daily notional value rising 43.3% to $1.1 trillion.
2026 Q2: SIFMA reported record US equity ADV of 20.2 billion shares and record options ADV of 72.8 million contracts.
2026 H1: PitchBook-NVCA reported US startups raised more than $400 billion, exceeding every prior full-year venture total on record.
outlook: Revenue should grow through 2026, but the mix is uneven. A reasonable industry-size estimate is about $70.5 billion in 2026 based on the 2022 IBISWorld projection path. Upside comes from AI dealmaking, improved IPO and M&A exits, higher trading volumes and continued derivatives activity. Downside risks include rate-sensitive valuations, a narrow LP fundraising market, weak distributions, tariff or geopolitical volatility that damages risk appetite, and regulatory scrutiny of market structure, private funds, AI and retail trading. The strongest operators will be scaled VC firms with durable LP access and trading firms with technology, data and balance-sheet advantages.

title: Veterinary Laboratory Testing Services
one_liner: Veterinary labs convert pet and livestock health demand into recurring diagnostic, pathology, molecular, imaging, and consultative testing revenue.
overview: This industry provides laboratory and diagnostic testing services for licensed veterinary practitioners, including bloodwork, urinalysis, pathology, microbiology, parasitology, molecular diagnostics, genetic testing, toxicology, radiography interpretation, and specialist consultation. The 2021 baseline file described a $9.2 billion market with 2021 growth of 0.4%, but the newer September 2024 IBISWorld reseller listing cites 2023 revenue of $12.4 billion after a 2018-2023 CAGR of 5.8%. For 2025, the market appears to have continued growing, but at a moderated pace as pet owners became more price-sensitive while diagnostic frequency, aging pets, pet insurance, and livestock surveillance kept testing volumes resilient.

major_players: University and state veterinary diagnostic laboratories
current_dynamics: The 2025 market is balancing resilient animal-health demand against consumer price sensitivity. APPA reported 2025 U.S. pet spending of $158 billion, up 3.7%, and projected 2026 spending of $165 billion, while IDEXX reported 2025 U.S. CAG diagnostics recurring revenue growth of 9% in Q4 2025, helped by higher diagnostic frequency and an aging pet population. At the same time, Zoetis reported a softer U.S. companion-animal environment in Q1 2026, with pet owners showing increased price sensitivity and veterinary visits declining. Livestock testing remains elevated by HPAI surveillance, including USDA-confirmed dairy cattle cases across 18 states since March 2024 and routine National Milk Testing Strategy testing in 2025.

whats_shrinking: 2025: low-complexity tests outsourced to reference labs when clinics can run them faster on in-house analyzers

outlook: The 2026 outlook is positive but more disciplined than the 2020-2023 rebound. Demand should keep expanding because pets are aging, cat and dog ownership remains broad, insured pets are increasing, and veterinarians are using diagnostics more often for preventive care and chronic disease management. Growth will be capped by clinic capacity limits, pet-owner price sensitivity, competition from in-house testing, and consolidation-driven pricing pressure. A reasonable 2026 U.S. revenue range is about $13.9 billion to $14.1 billion, implying roughly 3.5% to 5.0% growth from the estimated 2025 base.

title: Veterinary Services in the US
one_liner: Veterinary clinics are benefiting from resilient pet ownership, higher acuity care, pet insurance adoption and corporate consolidation, while affordability pressure and labor costs cap volume growth.
overview: The industry remains structurally supported by pet humanization, aging companion animals, broader availability of diagnostics and specialty procedures, and the need for livestock disease surveillance. The 2022 IBISWorld baseline put industry revenue at $61.4 billion after a pandemic-era demand surge; the most current public pet-spending data show veterinary care and products reached $41.4 billion in 2025, up from $39.8 billion in 2024, while total US pet expenditures reached $158 billion in 2025 and are projected at $165 billion in 2026. Demand is still healthy, but the mix is changing: households are prioritizing essential medical care, shopping harder on discretionary pet spending, and increasingly using insurance or financing for high-cost procedures.

how_it_makes_money: Revenue comes from exam fees, diagnostics, laboratory work, vaccinations, parasite control, dental care, nonsurgical treatment, surgery, emergency and specialty procedures, euthanasia and hospice, livestock health services, boarding or grooming add-ons, and in-clinic sales of medications, prescription diets and other merchandise. The 2022 baseline mix was led by nonsurgical treatments at 26.8% of revenue, routine examinations at 23.2%, laboratory services at 16.9%, surgical treatments at 14.9%, merchandise at 11.2%, boarding at 3.0%, other at 2.5% and grooming at 1.5%.
cost_structure: Veterinary practices are labor-intensive. Veterinarian, technician, assistant and front-office compensation is the largest cost pressure, with BLS/FRED labor compensation reaching $33.2 billion in 2025. Other major costs include pharmaceuticals, vaccines, diagnostic supplies, medical equipment, lab services, rent, utilities, insurance, software, payment processing, continuing education, regulatory compliance and corporate overhead for multi-site groups. Profitability is supported by private-pay demand and recurring wellness care, but pressured by wage inflation, high drug and supply costs, equipment investment, recruiting costs, tariff exposure on imported goods and clients trading down or delaying care when bills rise.
major_players: Mars Veterinary Health: Banfield Pet Hospital, VCA Animal Hospitals, BluePearl and Antech; more than 2,000 US veterinary hospitals and diagnostic providers cited in 2021-2025 company materials
National Veterinary Associates: JAB-backed consolidator with a large general, specialty and emergency footprint
Mission Pet Health: formed in 2025 from Southern Veterinary Partners and Mission Veterinary Partners
VetCor: private-equity-backed multi-site veterinary practice group
Thrive Pet Healthcare: TSG Consumer Partners-backed general, specialty and emergency operator
PetVet Care Centers: private-equity-backed multi-site veterinary operator
Independent veterinary hospitals: still a large share of locations, especially in companion-animal general practice
current_dynamics: Pet medical care remains a protected category in household budgets, but consumers are more value-conscious in 2025-2026. APPA reported 22% of pet owners spending less on pets in 2025, even as ownership stayed high and essential care held up. Clinics are responding with wellness plans, online pharmacies, pricing transparency, forward booking, extended hours, urgent-care formats and specialty referral networks. Corporate groups continue to gain scale through acquisition and branding, while independent clinics compete on local relationships, continuity of care and owner autonomy. Labor remains the main bottleneck: total compensation continues to rise, and debates about veterinarian and technician supply are shaping capacity, scheduling and wages.
whats_growing: Specialty and emergency care, preventive wellness plans, diagnostics, dentistry, oncology, dermatology, cardiology, chronic disease management for older pets, cat-related spending, pet insurance, online pharmacy fulfillment, direct-to-consumer scheduling tools, urgent-care clinic formats, mobile and in-home care, and livestock disease surveillance tied to HPAI and other animal health threats.
whats_shrinking: Discretionary visits and add-on services are more exposed where households face inflation and high veterinary bills. Lower-acuity services that can move to retail, online pharmacies or non-veterinary pet service providers face margin pressure. Independent ownership share is gradually shrinking as corporate and private-equity-backed groups acquire practices. Livestock-related demand can soften when cattle, dairy or poultry production cycles contract, though disease surveillance offsets some weakness.
recent_developments: 2025-01: Mars Veterinary Health reported sustainability progress including 100% renewable electricity across 2,300+ Banfield, BluePearl, Linnaeus and VCA clinics in the US and UK.
2025-04: NAPHIA reported US pet insurance premium volume of $4.74 billion for year-end 2024, with 6,405,541 insured US pets.
2025-07: Southern Veterinary Partners and Mission Veterinary Partners announced they had joined together as Mission Pet Health following a formal merger completed in late 2024.
2025-10: AVMA-reported pet owner economics showed veterinary care represented 32.4% of household pet-related expenditures in 2025 and the average last veterinary visit cost $200.
2026-03: APPA reported US pet industry expenditures reached $158 billion in 2025 and projected $165 billion for 2026, with 95 million pet-owning households in 2025.
2026-06: NAPHIA's 2026 industry data showed 7.6 million insured pets in North America at year-end 2025 and a 9% year-over-year increase in insured US pets.
outlook: The industry outlook is positive but slower and more uneven than the pandemic boom. Revenue growth should be supported by 2026 pet spending growth, pet insurance adoption, rising medical intensity per visit, specialty care, diagnostics and high pet ownership among younger households and Gen X. Constraints include affordability, labor availability, wage inflation, rising medical supply costs and consumer resistance to opaque pricing. Consolidation should continue, but regulatory and public scrutiny of private-equity rollups will keep increasing, especially in emergency and specialty markets. Clinics that can combine transparent pricing, convenient access, strong technician leverage, high medical quality and disciplined inventory/labor management are positioned best through 2026.
one_sentence: Veterinary Services in the US includes licensed veterinary practices and diagnostic labs that provide routine exams, nonsurgical treatment, surgery, lab work, dentistry, emergency care, specialty care and related products for companion and production animals.

title: Video Game Software Publishing in the US
one_liner: US video game software publishers are a mature-growth digital content market, with 2025 spending led by mobile, subscriptions, live services and a stronger premium release slate.
overview: Video game software publishing in the US has moved from a hit-driven packaged-goods model into a digitally distributed content and services market. The 2022 IBIS baseline estimated industry revenue at $41.924 billion after pandemic-era demand lifted playtime, digital downloads and mobile gaming. By 2025, US consumer spending on video game content reached $52.4 billion, up about 1.4% from restated 2024 content spending of $51.7 billion. Growth is no longer broad-based user expansion; it is increasingly coming from deeper monetization of existing players through subscriptions, live operations, premium releases, mobile in-app purchases and franchise ecosystems. Scale advantages remain large because major publishers control IP, marketing budgets, platform relationships, analytics and live-service infrastructure, while independent publishers still use Steam, console stores, mobile app stores and direct-to-consumer channels to reach niche audiences.

how_it_makes_money: Publishers earn from full-game sales, digital downloads, physical sell-in, mobile in-app purchases, DLC, microtransactions, battle passes, season passes, subscriptions, licensing, in-game advertising, platform incentives and IP extensions. Live-service games extend monetization after launch through recurring content drops, cosmetic items, multiplayer systems and virtual currencies, while subscription and cloud models shift some revenue from one-time purchases to recurring access fees.
cost_structure: The largest costs are software development labor, engineering, art, design, QA, server and cloud operations, platform fees, royalties, licensed IP, middleware, user acquisition, advertising, influencer and launch marketing, customer support, localization and corporate overhead. Digital distribution reduces physical manufacturing and retail costs, but high-end AAA production, live-service operations, talent competition, mobile user-acquisition costs and post-launch content pipelines keep fixed costs high.
major_players: Microsoft Gaming / Xbox Game Studios / Activision Blizzard King
Tencent-owned and Tencent-backed publishers active in the US market
current_dynamics: The US market is still growing, but the growth mix has changed. Content spending is near pandemic-era highs, while player-time expansion has slowed and competition for attention is intense. Mobile remains the largest content pool, subscriptions are one of the fastest-growing categories, and PC/console results are increasingly shaped by a smaller number of premium releases and long-running live-service titles. Consolidation has increased, with Microsoft absorbing Activision Blizzard and EA pursuing a $55 billion take-private transaction announced in 2025. Publishers are also rationalizing costs after over-expansion during the pandemic, even as they spend heavily on large franchises, cross-platform releases, AI-assisted production tools, creator economies and direct-to-consumer monetization.
whats_growing: 2025 US video game content spending, up to $52.4 billion from restated 2024 content spending of $51.7 billion.
2025 US subscription spending, up 20% year over year.
2025 US mobile game spending, up to $26.7 billion.
2025 global PC game revenue, with Newzoo reporting PC at $43.6 billion globally, up 12.0% year over year.
2025 premium PC and console spending, helped by stronger release slates and higher pricing.
Publisher-owned franchises with live operations, sports titles, user-generated content platforms and cross-platform communities.
whats_shrinking: Packaged physical distribution as digital downloads and live services take more sales share.
Console hardware momentum in parts of the market outside new platform launches, with Microsoft reporting Xbox hardware revenue down 25% in fiscal 2025.
Lower-performing live-service titles, especially where engagement is concentrated in a few franchises.
Undifferentiated mobile games facing higher user-acquisition costs and weaker organic discovery.
Small and mid-sized studios without durable IP, marketing scale or reliable platform visibility.
recent_developments: 2023-10-13: Microsoft completed its acquisition of Activision Blizzard, making Activision Blizzard King part of Microsoft Gaming.
2025-06-11: Nintendo said Switch 2 sold more than 3.5 million units worldwide in its first four days after its 2025-06-05 launch.
2025-09-29: Electronic Arts announced a definitive agreement to be acquired by a consortium led by PIF, Silver Lake and Affinity Partners at an enterprise value of about $55 billion.
2026-02-11: ESA, Circana and Sensor Tower reported 2025 US video game spending of about $60.8 billion, including $52.4 billion on content.
2026-05-05: Electronic Arts reported FY2026 net bookings of $8.026 billion, up 9% year over year.
2026-06-18: Newzoo reported 2025 global games revenue of $201.6 billion, up 9.1% year over year, with North America up 5.7%.
outlook: The 2026 outlook is positive but uneven. US content spending is positioned to benefit from a stronger premium release calendar, subscription price increases and tier upgrades, Switch 2 software demand, PC resilience and continuing mobile monetization. However, the market is mature, player attention is concentrated, and publishers face higher labor, development, server, licensing and marketing costs. The most defensible publishers will be those with durable IP, recurring player communities, multi-platform reach, disciplined release schedules and the ability to monetize after launch without over-relying on a single hit.
one_sentence: The industry publishes and monetizes games for console, PC, mobile, cloud and VR platforms, increasingly earning through digital downloads, subscriptions, DLC, microtransactions, advertising and cross-platform live services rather than packaged retail sales.
